name: Kings Canyon National Park
blurb: Giant sequoias, mule deer and the mountain lions of the high Sierra.

tip.title: Take away fire
tip.text: Sequoias need fire to open cones and clear rivals. Set Fire to -100% and watch sequoia, fireweed and the animals that rely on them.

sources.title: NPS: Mammals of Sequoia and Kings Canyon

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Short, snowy winters and bright summers set the growing season for plants from the foothills to the high country.

nodes.name: Snowpack & meltwater
nodes.desc: Heavy winter snow melts in May and June and feeds the streams and meadows. Streams usually shrink to a trickle by autumn.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.desc: Sequoias need periodic fire to open cones and clear competing growth. A century of fire suppression let fuel build up.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen needles, wood, carcasses and droppings and return nutrients to the forest soil.

nodes.name: Giant sequoia
nodes.desc: Grows in scattered groves on the western slope. Thick bark protects mature trees from fire, and fire clears the ground for seedlings.

nodes.name: California black oak
nodes.desc: A mid-elevation oak whose acorns and leaves feed deer, bears and rodents.

nodes.name: Thimbleberry
nodes.desc: A shrub with soft berries and leaves that deer browse and bears and other animals eat.

nodes.name: Fireweed
nodes.desc: A tall wildflower that spreads quickly across burned ground. Its nectar draws bees and deer browse it.

nodes.name: Meadow sedges & grasses
nodes.desc: Grass-like plants of Sierra meadows and high slopes that feed marmots, voles and bighorn sheep.

nodes.name: Mule deer
nodes.desc: Browses shrubs, wildflowers and oak. Wikipedia says that when predators declined in the early 1900s, deer numbers spiked and overgrazed the understory.

nodes.name: Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep
nodes.desc: An endangered high-country grazer of grasses and forbs that uses steep rocky ground to escape predators. Mountain lions are a major threat.

nodes.name: Yellow-bellied marmot
nodes.desc: A large ground squirrel of meadows and talus that eats grasses and wildflowers and hibernates through winter.

nodes.name: Golden-mantled ground squirrel
nodes.desc: Eats seeds, fungi, fruit and insects, and is prey for hawks and bears.

nodes.name: Douglas squirrel
nodes.desc: Wikipedia says it gnaws young sequoia cones year-round, dropping some seeds as it feeds.

nodes.name: Long-tailed vole
nodes.desc: A small rodent of damp meadows that eats grasses and other green plants and is prey for hawks.

nodes.name: Deer mouse
nodes.desc: An abundant small rodent that eats seeds and insects and is prey for hawks and snakes.

nodes.name: Bumble bees
nodes.desc: Several bumble bee species feed on flower nectar and pollen, and visit wildflowers such as fireweed.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats berries, nuts, insects, carrion and young deer. In the park it often seeks human food near campgrounds.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: A clever omnivore and scavenger and the most recorded bird in the area. It picks over carcasses.

nodes.name: Red-tailed hawk
nodes.desc: Hunts squirrels, marmots, mice and voles from the air, and has the widest list of prey recorded in GloBI here.

nodes.name: Northern Pacific rattlesnake
nodes.desc: Ambushes mice, small marmots and lizards on warm, rocky slopes.

nodes.name: Mountain lion
nodes.desc: The park's main large predator. It hunts mule deer and is a major threat to Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep.
